headline: New law imposes up to 5 years in prison for exam malpractice in Bangladesh
summary: A new law in Bangladesh introduces strict penalties for examiners involved in unfair marking and digital manipulation.
details: Today, Bangladesh's Parliament passed the Public Examinations (Offences) (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which introduces severe penalties for examiners involved in unfair marking practices. Under the new law, examiners who deliberately award incorrect marks may face up to two years' imprisonment.

The bill amends the Public Examinations (Offences) Act of 1980, which has been deemed outdated due to the rise of digital exam malpractice. It now includes a definition for 'digital manipulation' and prescribes penalties for unauthorized access to examination databases.

In addition to penalties for unfair marking, the legislation also addresses organized examination crimes, making it illegal to facilitate cheating in public examinations. Offenders may face up to five years' imprisonment and fines.

The law also includes protections for whistleblowers who report examination-related offences, ensuring their identities are safeguarded from retaliation. This aims to encourage reporting of malpractice in the education system.
caption:
Bangladesh's Parliament has passed a landmark bill imposing severe penalties for exam malpractice. What does this mean for the education system?

Today, Bangladesh's Parliament passed the Public Examinations (Offences) (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which introduces severe penalties for examiners involved in unfair marking practices. Under the new law, examiners who deliberately award incorrect marks may face up to two years' imprisonment.

The bill amends the Public Examinations (Offences) Act of 1980, which has been deemed outdated due to the rise of digital exam malpractice. It now includes a definition for 'digital manipulation' and prescribes penalties for unauthorized access to examination databases.

In addition to penalties for unfair marking, the legislation also addresses organized examination crimes, making it illegal to facilitate cheating in public examinations. Offenders may face up to five years' imprisonment and fines.

The law also includes protections for whistleblowers who report examination-related offences, ensuring their identities are safeguarded from retaliation. This aims to encourage reporting of malpractice in the education system.

headline: Floodwater disrupts road link between Chattogram and hill districts
summary: Heavy rain has submerged a section of the Chattogram-Ramgarh highway, leaving buses and trucks stranded and passengers wading through waist-deep water.
details: Road communication between Chattogram and the hill districts of Rangamati and Khagrachhari was disrupted after floodwater submerged a section of the Chattogram-Ramgarh highway at Barodighir Par in Hathazari.

The road went under water around noon, causing severe traffic congestion on both sides of the flooded stretch. Buses, trucks, and smaller vehicles were stranded, while many passengers were forced to wade through waist-deep water to find alternative transport.
The Chattogram-Ramgarh highway is a critical route linking Chattogram with Rangamati, Khagrachhari, and the upazilas of Hathazari, Fatikchhari, Raozan, and Rangunia.
A driver on the Chattogram-Rangamati route reported that water entered his bus and stalled the engine as he attempted to cross the submerged road.
A journalist traveling from Fatikchhari to Chattogram city described the road as looking like a canal, noting that the edges of the road were no longer visible, increasing the risk of accidents.
Muslem Uddin, executive engineer of the Chattogram Roads and Highways Department, stated that floodwater from a nearby wetland and surrounding hilly areas inundated the highway.
Department officials have visited the area and will conduct a full inspection of the road once the water recedes.
caption:
Roads turned into canals: Floodwater has cut off the link between Chattogram and the hill districts.

Road communication between Chattogram and the hill districts of Rangamati and Khagrachhari was disrupted after floodwater submerged a section of the Chattogram-Ramgarh highway at Barodighir Par in Hathazari.

The road went under water around noon, causing severe traffic congestion on both sides of the flooded stretch. Buses, trucks, and smaller vehicles were stranded, while many passengers were forced to wade through waist-deep water to find alternative transport.

The Chattogram-Ramgarh highway is a critical route linking Chattogram with Rangamati, Khagrachhari, and the upazilas of Hathazari, Fatikchhari, Raozan, and Rangunia.

A driver on the Chattogram-Rangamati route reported that water entered his bus and stalled the engine as he attempted to cross the submerged road.

A journalist traveling from Fatikchhari to Chattogram city described the road as looking like a canal, noting that the edges of the road were no longer visible, increasing the risk of accidents.

Muslem Uddin, executive engineer of the Chattogram Roads and Highways Department, stated that floodwater from a nearby wetland and surrounding hilly areas inundated the highway.

Department officials have visited the area and will conduct a full inspection of the road once the water recedes.
